lesson.menu_desc: Comparing the town you chose with the city you left -- with the boosters that make a comparison B2
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 2 -- A Town of 40,000
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Claudia Veraldi | Lesson 2 -- A Town of 40,000

listenings.text: Everybody warned me that I would be bored. I had lived in Oslo for nineteen years, and when I told people I was moving to a town two hours away, they looked at me as if I had lost my mind. They said I would miss the amenities. The truth is the opposite. This town has a hospital, two supermarkets, a cinema and a very good library. It has everything except the crowds. It is nowhere near as busy as Oslo, and it is considerably cheaper. My apartment in the city cost more than this whole house. Is it far quieter? Yes. It is far quieter than anywhere I had lived before, and that is exactly why I came. There is a trade-off, of course. There are fewer concerts, and the airport is a long drive. But the quiet more than makes up for it. Nobody here is in a hurry, and after nineteen years of hurrying, that is worth a great deal.

Everyone assumes I miss it. I grew up in a town of about thirty thousand people, and I could not wait to leave. When you grow up somewhere that small, everybody knows everything about you before you have decided it yourself. I wanted to be one face among millions, and that is exactly what the city gave me. People talk about the quiet as if it were a gift. Honestly, I think it is overrated. My town was not laid-back, it was slow, and there was nothing at all to do after eight in the evening. Does the city cost me something? Of course it does. I live in a cramped apartment I can barely afford, and I put up with a commute that eats an hour of every day. That is the trade-off, and I would make it again tomorrow.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: So small that there is no room to move comfortably
A good thing you give up in order to get another good thing
The useful services a place offers, like shops and transport
Spreading out over a very large area, with no clear end
To accept something annoying without complaining about it
Cheap enough for an ordinary person to pay without difficulty

vocab.text: The last two words of this lesson are not single words at all: the middle of nowhere and the best of both worlds are whole phrases. Keep them intact, exactly as they are, and you will sound like somebody who has spoken English for years.

paras: Ask anybody in a capital city to picture a town of forty thousand people and they will describe a place with one street, one bakery and nothing else. They picture the middle of nowhere. In reality a town that size usually has a hospital, several schools, a bus network, a market and more restaurants than one person can visit in a year. It has, in other words, every amenity an ordinary life needs.

What it does not have is the crowd. A town of forty thousand is nowhere near as busy as a sprawling capital, and that is precisely the point. Housing is considerably more affordable, because nobody is bidding against four million other people for the same apartment. Families who spent years in cramped apartments find themselves in houses three times the size, with a garden, for less than half the price.

There is a trade-off, and honest people name it. The airport is farther. The concert you wanted to see will not come. Specialist medicine sometimes means a long drive. Anybody who tells you a small town costs them nothing is selling something.

But the people who make this move rarely regret it, and their reason is almost always the same. The pace is slower, the neighbors are more laid-back, and the noise that everybody in the city puts up with simply is not there. By far the most common sentence you hear from them is not about money or space. It is this: I did not know how loud my old life was until it stopped.

reading.prompt: Read once, quickly. Which title fits the whole text best?
choices: Why small towns are cheaper than capitals
A town of forty thousand has what a life needs, and costs a real trade-off

items: People in capital cities usually imagine a town of forty thousand as bigger than it is.
The opposite: they picture one street, one bakery and nothing else — the middle of nowhere.
According to the text, a town that size normally has a hospital and several schools.
The first paragraph lists a hospital, several schools, a bus network, a market and restaurants.
Housing is cheaper because the houses are smaller.
It is cheaper because nobody is bidding against four million other people. The houses are three times bigger.
The text says the move costs nothing.
It names the trade-off directly: a farther airport, concerts that never come, and long drives for specialist medicine.
The most common thing these people say is about how loud their old life was.
The last line: I did not know how loud my old life was until it stopped.

items.situation: A colleague in New York asks: so how big is this town of yours? Answer, and make the size feel deliberate rather than small.
tips: Forty thousand — nowhere near as big as Sao Paulo, and that was the point.
Give one number and one advantage in the same sentence.

items.situation: Somebody says: houses must be dirt cheap out there. Answer without sounding like you moved only for money.
tips: They are considerably more affordable, but that was not the reason.
Name the real reason right after the price.

items.situation: A friend from London asks what you gave up. Name the trade-off honestly.
tips: The airport is two hours away, and some things simply do not come here.
Then say what makes up for it.

items.situation: A Norwegian colleague says, politely, that he could never live so far from a city. Disagree without contradicting him flatly.
tips: I can see why it would not suit everyone.
That is fair — for me the quiet more than makes up for it.

items.situation: Somebody calls your town the middle of nowhere. Correct them, lightly.
tips: It is nowhere near as remote as people assume.
We have every amenity, just no queues.

items.situation: You are asked: what is the one thing the capital still does better?
tips: The capital is by far the better place for that.

answerkey.title: Reveal the whole booster key
key: far / much + comparative = a big gap: it is far quieter
considerably / significantly = the same, more formal: considerably more affordable
slightly / a little = a small gap: slightly colder in winter
not nearly as ... as = much less, and the gap is huge
nowhere near as ... as = the same, stronger and more spoken
by far + the superlative = first place, with nobody close
the -er, the -er = two things moving together: the smaller the town, the faster you know everyone
NEVER: more quieter, very cheaper, as busy than, the most best
